title: The mole: one number links mass, particles and gas volume

blocks.text: Atoms in a molecule sample = moles × Nₐ × atoms per formula. Example: 9 g H₂O = 0.5 mol = 3.01 × 10²³ molecules but 9.03 × 10²³ atoms.
Read the question: molecules, atoms or ions? 1 mol H₂SO₄ holds 4 mol O atoms; 1 mol CaCl₂ gives 3 mol ions.

title: Isotopes, average atomic mass and the mass spectrometer

blocks.text: Average relative atomic mass = Σ(isotope mass × % abundance) / 100.
Mass spectrometer

items: Atoms are ionised, accelerated through voltage V, then bent by magnetic field B.
m/e = B²r² / 2V, so radius r ∝ √(m/e).
Smaller m/e (lighter or more highly charged ion) → smaller radius, bent most.
Each peak = one isotope; peak height = relative abundance.

blocks.text: Average mass always lies between the isotope masses, closer to the more abundant one.

title: Combustion analysis to empirical and molecular formula

items: Mass of C = (12/44) × mass of CO₂
Mass of H = (2/18) × mass of H₂O
Mass of O = sample mass − (C + H)
Divide each by its atomic mass, then by the smallest → whole-number ratio = empirical formula
n = molar mass / empirical formula mass; molecular formula = n × empirical

blocks.text: Ratio ends in .5 → ×2; in .33 or .67 → ×3.
Moles of CO₂ = moles of C; moles of H₂O × 2 = moles of H. With moles of compound known, divide straight away: 0.1 mol CₓHᵧ giving 0.4 mol CO₂ means x = 4.
Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ and methanal HCHO share the empirical formula CH₂O.

items: Change every reactant to moles.
Divide each by its coefficient in the balanced equation.
Smallest answer = limiting reactant; it decides how much product forms.
The other reactant is in excess: some is left over.

blocks.text: Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 2 mol H₂ and 2 mol O₂: H₂ 2/2 = 1, O₂ 2/1 = 2 → H₂ limits; 2 mol H₂O form, 1 mol O₂ is left.
% yield = actual yield / theoretical yield × 100
The reactant with fewer moles is not always limiting: compare moles ÷ coefficient. Actual yield is normally less than theoretical (side reactions, losses).

title: Kinetic molecular theory: postulates and results

items: Molecules are tiny; their own volume is negligible.
They move randomly in straight lines and collide elastically (no loss of total KE).
No attractions or repulsions between them.
Pressure comes from collisions with the walls.
Average KE ∝ absolute temperature.

head: Result
Formula
rows: PV = ⅓ mNc̄² (N = number of molecules, c̄² = mean square speed)

blocks.text: At the same T every gas has the same average KE; lighter molecules simply move faster.

title: Real gases, van der Waals, liquefaction and plasma

blocks.text: Real gases deviate most at high pressure and low temperature; they behave most ideally at low P and high T. H₂ and He are closest to ideal.
(P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT

items: a: corrects for attractions (atm dm⁶ mol⁻²); larger for polar or big molecules, e.g. NH₃, SO₂ ≫ N₂ > H₂ > He
b: corrects for the volume of the molecules (dm³ mol⁻¹)
Liquefaction: cool below the critical temperature, then compress. Linde's method uses Joule–Thomson cooling (expansion from high to low pressure).
Plasma: ionised gas of ions and electrons, overall neutral, conducts electricity (lightning, neon signs, the Sun).

blocks.text: Above its critical temperature a gas cannot be liquefied, however high the pressure.

title: Bohr model and the hydrogen spectrum

head: Quantity
Hydrogen atom
rows: rₙ = 0.529 n² Å (÷ Z for He⁺, Li²⁺)
Eₙ = −1312/n² kJ mol⁻¹ = −13.6/n² eV (× Z² for He⁺, Li²⁺)

blocks.text: Series (electron falls to n₁): Lyman 1 (UV), Balmer 2 (visible), Paschen 3, Brackett 4, Pfund 5 (infrared).
Moseley: √(X-ray frequency) ∝ atomic number Z, so elements are ordered by Z.
Third orbit radius = 9 × 0.529 = 4.76 Å. Energy gaps shrink as n grows.

items: Shell n holds n² orbitals and 2n² electrons.
Subshell holds 2(2l + 1): s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.
s spherical; p dumbbell (pₓ has the yz plane as its node); d mostly four-lobed.
Nodes: angular = l, radial = n − l − 1.

blocks.text: l can never equal n: there is no 1p or 2d orbital.

items: Aufbau (n + l) rule: lower n + l fills first; if equal, lower n first.
Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s 4f 5d 6p
Pauli: no two electrons share all four quantum numbers → at most 2 per orbital, opposite spins.
Hund: in p, d or f orbitals put electrons in singly, spins parallel, before pairing.

blocks.text: Exceptions: Cr [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ (half-filled and full d are extra stable).
✔ Fe²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁶ (4s electrons leave first). ✘ [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².
N (2p³) has 3 unpaired electrons; O (2p⁴) has 2.
Repulsion: lone–lone > lone–bond > bond–bond. Each lone pair squeezes the bond angle.
Angle order: CH₄ (109.5°) > NH₃ (≈107°) > H₂O (104.5°).

items: Single bond = 1σ; double = 1σ + 1π; triple = 1σ + 2π.
σ: head-on overlap (stronger); π: sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals.
C₂H₄: 5σ, 1π. C₂H₂: 3σ, 2π.

blocks.text: More s-character → shorter C–H bond and more electronegative carbon (sp > sp² > sp³).

title: Molecular orbitals: bond order and magnetism

blocks.text: Bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) / 2. Unpaired electrons → paramagnetic.
Higher bond order → stronger, shorter bond: O₂⁺ > O₂ > O₂⁻ > O₂²⁻ in strength.
Lewis structures make O₂ look all-paired; only MO theory explains its paramagnetism.

title: Bond types, polarity, dipole moment, bond length

items: Pauling electronegativity: F 4.0 > O 3.5 > N 3.0 = Cl 3.0 > C 2.5 > H 2.1
Difference about 1.7 or more → mostly ionic; smaller → polar covalent; zero → non-polar
Coordinate bond: both electrons from one atom (NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃)
Dipole moment μ = q × r, unit debye (1 D = 3.34 × 10⁻³⁰ C m)

blocks.text: Bond length: C–C 1.54 Å > C=C 1.34 Å > C≡C 1.20 Å. Bond energy: H–F > H–Cl > H–Br > H–I (longer bond, weaker).
CO₂ has polar bonds but zero dipole moment: the bond dipoles cancel.

title: First law, internal energy and enthalpy

items: State functions (E, H, P, V, T) depend only on start and end; q and w do not.
Exothermic: ΔH −. Endothermic: ΔH +.
First law: ΔE = q + w (w = work done on the system).
ΔH = ΔE + PΔV; for gases ΔH = ΔE + ΔnRT (Δn = gas moles of products − reactants).
Constant volume: qᵥ = ΔE. Constant pressure: qₚ = ΔH.

blocks.text: Books sign work two ways; just count energy in as +, out as −. A gas absorbing 300 J of heat and doing 120 J of work on the surroundings: ΔE = 300 − 120 = +180 J.
Spontaneous ≠ exothermic: ice melts on its own above 0 °C yet absorbs heat.
Standard conditions: 298 K, 1 atm (newer books: 1 bar), 1 mol dm⁻³ solutions; substances in their standard states.

blocks.text: Weak acid or weak base: neutralisation is less exothermic than −57 kJ mol⁻¹, because some energy goes to ionise it.
Moles of water formed = moles of the reactant (H⁺ or OH⁻) that runs out.

items: Heat q = m c ΔT (water: c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
ΔH = −q / moles reacted (minus sign: heat gained by water came from the reaction)
Glass (coffee-cup) calorimeter: constant pressure → ΔH
Bomb calorimeter: constant volume → ΔE; q = heat capacity × ΔT

blocks.text: Hess's law

items: Total ΔH is the same by any route.
ΔH(reaction) = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants)
Reverse an equation → change the sign of ΔH.
Multiply an equation by 2 → multiply ΔH by 2.

blocks.text: Heat lost from a simple calorimeter makes a measured exothermic ΔH less negative than the true value.

title: Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, and ΔG

items: Na(s) → Na(g): sublimation +108
Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻: ionisation energy +496
½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g): ½ bond energy +121
Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g): electron affinity −349
Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s): lattice energy −787
Sum = ΔHf(NaCl) = −411 kJ mol⁻¹

blocks.text: Lattice energy is the one step that cannot be measured directly; the cycle gives it from ΔHf and the other steps.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; spontaneous when ΔG < 0. ΔH −, ΔS +: always. ΔH +, ΔS −: never. Signs mixed: depends on T (switches at T = ΔH/ΔS).
ΔS is usually in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹: convert before dividing.

title: Law of mass action, Kc and Kp

items: Kc = k(forward) / k(reverse)
Leave out pure solids and pure liquids.
Kp = Kc (RT)^Δn, Δn = gas moles of products − gas moles of reactants
Δn = 0 (e.g. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI): Kp = Kc, no units, and the volume cancels
Units of Kc: (mol dm⁻³)^Δn

blocks.text: K changes only with temperature, never with concentration, pressure or a catalyst.
A system at equilibrium shifts to undo a change made to it.

K changes?

If gas moles are equal on both sides, pressure has no effect on the position.

items: Low T favours yield but is too slow, so a moderate T plus a catalyst is the compromise.
SO₃ is absorbed in 98 % H₂SO₄ to give oleum H₂S₂O₇, then diluted; SO₃ straight into water makes an acid mist.

blocks.text: The contact process yield is already high at low pressure, so high pressure is not worth its cost.

Dynamic: both reactions keep going (radioactive I₂ added soon shows up in HI).
Reached from either side, only in a closed vessel.

Basic buffer: weak base + its salt (NH₄OH + NH₄Cl): pOH = pKb + log([salt]/[base])
Acidic buffer: added H⁺ is taken up by the salt's anion, added OH⁻ by the weak acid. Basic buffer: added H⁺ by the weak base, added OH⁻ by the salt's cation (NH₄⁺).

title: Galvanic cells, SHE and the electrochemical series

items: SHE: Pt, H₂ at 1 atm, 1 M H⁺, 25 °C; E° = 0.00 V by convention.

items: k = A e^(−Ea/RT)

Ea = energy of the peak (activated complex) − energy of reactants
Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH

blocks.text: Example: reactants 50, peak 150, products 20 kJ mol⁻¹ → Ea(forward) = 100, Ea(reverse) = 130, ΔH = −30.
Near room temperature a 10 K rise roughly doubles the rate, mainly because many more molecules reach Ea.
A catalyst lowers Ea of both directions by the same amount; ΔH does not change.
